case.case_title: Senasinghe v. Karunatilleke, Senior Superintendent of Police, Nugegoda and others
case.source_citation: [2003] 1 Sri L.R. 172, Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, SC No. 431/2001 (FR), decided on 17 March 2003

clause.text: No person shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the petitioner was subjected to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment in violation of Article 11 of the Constitution when police officers, under orders of the 1st Respondent, fired rubber bullets at him during a protest march.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner claimed he was not a participant in the protest march but a bystander, and that police officers fired rubber bullets at him causing serious injuries, thus violating his rights under Article 11.
case_context.respondent_argument: The 1st Respondent argued the protest march was unlawful under section 45 of the Referendum Act, that the petitioner was a willing participant, and that the police used reasonable force to disperse the crowd, denying that the petitioner suffered serious injury or was unlawfully arrested.
key_facts: The petitioner was injured by rubber bullets fired by police during a protest march on 19.7.2001.
The police acted under section 45 of the Referendum Act which prohibited processions during the Referendum period.
The petitioner was not a participant in the protest but a bystander trying to return to his car.
The 1st Respondent ordered police to fire rubber bullets, including at the petitioner, causing serious injuries requiring surgery.
The police actions were contrary to Police Departmental Orders regarding use of firearms.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The Court held that Article 11 prohibits cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment, and that the police use of rubber bullets on the petitioner, who was a bystander and not advancing towards police, constituted cruel and inhuman treatment. The Court emphasized that police must use minimal force and comply with departmental rules, which were violated here.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The petitioner was shot at close range while moving away from police, with no justification under the Police Departmental Orders. The firing was not related to dispersing protesters and showed callous disregard for the petitioner's safety, thus violating Article 11.
principles_established: Police use of force must be reasonable, necessary, and comply with departmental rules.
Article 11 protects individuals from cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment by state actors.
Bystanders are protected under Article 11 from excessive police force.
Judicial review extends to police conduct violating fundamental rights.
precedents_cited: West Virginia State Board of Education v Barnette (1943) 319 US 624

outcome.holding: The Court held that the 1st Respondent violated Article 11 by ordering police to fire rubber bullets at the petitioner, subjecting him to cruel and inhuman treatment.
outcome.remedy_or_orders: The Court awarded the petitioner Rs 200,000 in compensation for the infringement of Article 11, and ordered the 1st Respondent to personally pay Rs 20,000 with the State paying the balance.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 11 was central to the Court's finding that the police conduct in firing rubber bullets at the petitioner constituted cruel and inhuman treatment, violating his fundamental rights and justifying compensation.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The petitioner was shot at close range with rubber bullets by police officers on orders of the 1st Respondent, causing serious injuries requiring surgery, contrary to Police Departmental Orders.
